## Learning objectives
\Large
By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

* Explain over-training and over-smoothing using kNN
* Describe K-fold cross-validation and the bootstrap
* Use cross-validation to choose a tuning parameter
* Fit and tune models with caret's `train` function
* Use CV to develop a TB gene-expression biomarker, and avoid selection bias

## Cross-validation 
\Large
__Cross-validation__ is one of the most important ideas in machine learning. We start with the concepts and math, then implement it with `caret`.

## K-nearest neighbors (kNN)
To motivate cross-validation, we start with a real algorithm: __k-nearest neighbors (kNN)__.
\center
![](cvfigs/KnnClassification.svg.png){width=40%}


## K-nearest neighbors (kNN)
\center
![](cvfigs/knn.png){width=60%}

## K-nearest neighbors (kNN)
\Large
kNN estimates the conditional probability
$$p(x_1, x_2) = \mbox{Pr}(Y=1 \mid X_1=x_1 , X_2 = x_2).$$
For any point $(x_1,x_2)$:

1. Find the $k$ nearest training points (the _neighborhood_)
2. Average their 0s and 1s to get $\hat{p}(x_1,x_2)$



## K-nearest neighbors (kNN)
\center
Using _k=1_: \    \   \   \   \   \   \   \   \   \  \    \    and _k_=5:

![](cvfigs/Map1NN.png){width=49%} 
![](cvfigs/Map5NN.png){width=49%} 


## K-nearest neighbors (kNN): Example
Using the following dataset:
\small
```{r mnist-27-data, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="60%", fig.align="center"}
library(dslabs); data("mnist_27")
mnist_27$test %>% ggplot(aes(x_1, x_2, color = y)) + geom_point()
```

## K-nearest neighbors (kNN): Example
\Large
Fit kNN with $k=5$ using `caret::knn3`:

```{r, eval=TRUE}
library(caret)
knn_fit <- knn3(y ~ ., data = mnist_27$train, k = 5)
```

## K-nearest neighbors (kNN): Example
\Large
The classes are balanced, so we use accuracy to measure performance. `type = "class"` returns predicted labels:
\small
```{r}
y_hat_knn <- predict(knn_fit, mnist_27$test, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn, mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```

## K-nearest neighbors (kNN): Example

```{r knn-fit, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
# We use this function to plot the estimated conditional probabilities
plot_cond_prob <- function(p_hat=NULL){
  tmp <- mnist_27$true_p
  if(!is.null(p_hat)){
    tmp <- mutate(tmp, p=p_hat)
  }
  tmp %>% ggplot(aes(x_1, x_2, z=p, fill=p)) +
  geom_raster(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=c("#F8766D","white","#00BFC4")) +
  stat_contour(breaks=c(0.5),color="black")
}

p1 <- plot_cond_prob() + ggtitle("True conditional probability")

p2 <- plot_cond_prob(predict(knn_fit, mnist_27$true_p)[,2]) +
  ggtitle("kNN-5 estimate")
library(gridExtra)

grid.arrange(p2, p1, nrow=1)
``` 

## Over-training
**Over-training** (over-fitting): accuracy is higher on the training set than on the test set:
\small
```{r}
y_hat_knn <- predict(knn_fit, mnist_27$train, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn, mnist_27$train$y)$overall["Accuracy"]

y_hat_knn <- predict(knn_fit, mnist_27$test, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn, mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```


## Over-training 

Over-training is worst with $k=1$:
\small
```{r}
knn_fit_1 <- knn3(y ~ ., data = mnist_27$train, k = 1)
y_hat_knn_1 <- predict(knn_fit_1, mnist_27$train, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn_1, mnist_27$train$y)$overall[["Accuracy"]]
```

\small
```{r}
y_hat_knn_1 <- predict(knn_fit_1, mnist_27$test, type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn_1, mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```

## Over-training 
With $k=1$, the boundary traces every training point:
```{r knn-1-overfit, echo=F, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
p1 <- mnist_27$true_p %>% 
  mutate(knn = predict(knn_fit_1, newdata = .)[,2]) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = mnist_27$train, aes(x_1, x_2, color= y),
             pch=21, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=c("#F8766D","white","#00BFC4")) +
  stat_contour(aes(x_1, x_2, z = knn), breaks=c(0.5), color="black") +
  ggtitle("Train set")

p2 <- mnist_27$true_p %>% 
  mutate(knn = predict(knn_fit_1, newdata = .)[,2]) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = mnist_27$test, aes(x_1, x_2, color= y), 
             pch=21, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=c("#F8766D","white","#00BFC4")) +
  stat_contour(aes(x_1, x_2, z = knn), breaks=c(0.5), color="black") +
  ggtitle("Test set")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow=1)
``` 

## Over-smoothing

$k=5$ is also over-trained, though less than $k=1$. What about a much larger $k$, such as $k=401$?

\small
```{r}
knn_fit_401 <- knn3(y ~ ., data = mnist_27$train, k = 401)
y_hat_knn_401 <- predict(knn_fit_401, mnist_27$test, 
                         type = "class")
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn_401, mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```

## Over-smoothing
```{r mnist-27-glm-est, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6, out.width="70%",fig.align="center"}

p1 <- plot_cond_prob(predict(knn_fit_1, mnist_27$true_p)[,2]) +
  ggtitle("kNN-1")

p2 <- plot_cond_prob(predict(knn_fit, mnist_27$true_p)[,2]) +
  ggtitle("kNN-5")

p3 <- plot_cond_prob(predict(knn_fit_401, mnist_27$true_p)[,2]) +
  ggtitle("kNN-401")
  
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, nrow=1)
```



## Picking the $k$ in kNN
\Large
We want the $k$ that maximizes accuracy (or minimizes expected MSE). **Cross validation** estimates these quantities for any algorithm and tuning parameter.

To see why we need it, try many values of $k$:

```{r}
ks <- seq(3, 251, 2)
```

## Picking the $k$ in kNN
Use `map_df` to compute train and test accuracy for each $k$:
\small
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(purrr)
accuracy <- map_df(ks, function(k){
  fit <- knn3(y ~ ., data = mnist_27$train, k = k)
  
  y_hat <- predict(fit, mnist_27$train, type = "class")
  cm_train <- confusionMatrix(y_hat, mnist_27$train$y)
  train_error <- cm_train$overall["Accuracy"]
  
  y_hat <- predict(fit, mnist_27$test, type = "class")
  cm_test <- confusionMatrix(y_hat, mnist_27$test$y)
  test_error <- cm_test$overall["Accuracy"]
  
  tibble(train = train_error, test = test_error)
})
```

## Picking the $k$ in kNN
\Large
Accuracy for each $k$:

```{r accuracy-vs-k-knn, echo=FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="65%",fig.align="center"}
accuracy %>% mutate(k = ks) %>%
  gather(set, accuracy, -k) %>%
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("train", "test"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(k, accuracy, color = set)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() 
```

## Picking the $k$ in kNN
\Large
Picking $k$ this way uses the test set, so this accuracy is over-optimistic:

```{r}
ks[which.max(accuracy$test)]
max(accuracy$test)
```

## Mathematical description of cross validation
\Large
Goal: find predictions $\hat{Y}$ for outcome $Y$ that minimize the MSE:

$$
\mbox{MSE} = \mbox{E}\left\{ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{Y}_i - Y_i)^2 \right\}
$$

## Mathematical description of cross validation
\Large
With only one dataset, we estimate it with the observed MSE:

$$
\hat{\mbox{MSE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2
$$
These are the _true error_ and the _apparent error_.

## Mathematical description of cross validation
\Large
Two problems with the apparent error:

1. It is a random variable: one algorithm can beat another by luck.
2. If we train and evaluate on the same data, we overtrain (as with $k=1$).

## Mathematical description of cross validation
\Large
**Cross validation** addresses both. Think of the true error as the average apparent error over $B$ new random samples, none used for training:
$$\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(\hat{y}_i^b - y_i^b\right)^2 $$
with $B$ practically infinite.

## Mathematical description of cross validation
\Large
In practice we only have one set of outcomes, $y_1, \dots, y_n$. Cross validation imitates this setup by generating many random samples from the data we have.

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
We start with a dataset (blue) and want an algorithm that works on independent validation data (yellow).
\center
![](cvfigs/cv-1.png){height=50%}

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
But we never see the independent data.
\center
![](cvfigs/cv-2.png){height=50%}

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
So we split off a __training set__ (blue) and a __test set__ (red). Train only on the training set; use the test set only for evaluation.
\center
![](cvfigs/cv-3.png){height=50%}

<!--
## K-fold cross validation
We usually try to select a small piece of the dataset so that we have as much data as possible to train. However, we also want the test set to be large so that we obtain a stable estimate of the loss without fitting an impractical number of models. Typical choices are to use 10%-20% of the data for testing.
-->

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
We need to tune parameters ($\lambda$) without touching the test set, and tuning and evaluating on the same data overtrains.

Cross validation estimates the MSE for each candidate $\lambda$; we pick the smallest.

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
For a fixed $\lambda$, we want to imitate
$$\mbox{MSE}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(\hat{y}_i^b(\lambda) - y_i^b\right)^2 $$

K-fold cross validation creates $K$ pseudo-independent samples. Here $K=5$.

## K-fold cross validation
\Large Pick $M=N/K$ observations at random as the _validation set_ $y_1^b, \dots, y_M^b$ (here $b=1$):

\center
![](cvfigs/cv-4.png){height=50%}

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
Fit on the rest of the training set, then compute the error on the validation set:
$$\hat{\mbox{MSE}}_b(\lambda) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M \left(\hat{y}_i^b(\lambda) - y_i^b\right)^2 $$

## K-fold cross validation
Split the observations into $K$ non-overlapping folds:

\center
![](cvfigs/cv-5.png){height=40%}

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
Repeat for each fold $b=1,\dots,K$ and average:

$$
\hat{\mbox{MSE}}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{b=1}^K \hat{\mbox{MSE}}_b(\lambda)
$$

Then pick the $\lambda$ that minimizes $\hat{\mbox{MSE}}(\lambda)$.

## K-fold cross validation
Tuning used the training data, so evaluate the final model on the test set:

\center
![](cvfigs/cv-6.png){height=50%}

## K-fold cross validation
Or cross validate the whole procedure again:

\center
![](cvfigs/cv-7.png){height=65%}

## K-fold cross validation

\center
![](cvfigs/cv-8.png){height=65%}

## K-fold cross validation
\Large 
Choosing $K$:

* Larger $K$: training folds look more like the full data
* But slower: 100-fold is 10x slower than 10-fold
* $K=5$ and $K=10$ are popular choices

## K-fold cross validation
\Large
To reduce variance, we can take more samples: pick sets of observations at random instead of fixed folds.

Sampling **with replacement** is the _bootstrap_, and it is the default in __caret__. Here is how the bootstrap works in general.

## Bootstrap

Suppose the income distribution of your population is as follows:

```{r income-distribution,  fig.align="center"}
set.seed(1995)
n <- 10^6
income <- 10^(rnorm(n, log10(45000), log10(3)))
qplot(log10(income), bins = 30, color = I("black"))
```

## Bootstrap
\Large
The population median is: 

```{r}
m <- median(income)
m
```

## Bootstrap
\Large
In practice we only have a sample. Estimate $m$ with the median $M$ of a sample of 100:

```{r}
N <- 100
X <- sample(income, N)
median(X)
```

How to construct a CI? What is the distribution of $M$?

## Bootstrap
We can use a Monte Carlo simulation to learn the distribution of $M$.
\small
```{r median-is-normal, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="30%", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3, fig.align="center"}
library(gridExtra)
B <- 10^4
M <- replicate(B, {X <- sample(income, N); median(X)})
p1 <- qplot(M, bins = 30, color = I("black"))
p2 <- qplot(sample = scale(M), xlab = "theoretical", 
            ylab = "sample") + geom_abline()
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

## Bootstrap
\Large
In practice we don't know this distribution. A 95% CI based on the CLT:

```{r}
median(X) + 1.96 * sd(X) / sqrt(N) * c(-1, 1)
```

## Bootstrap
\Large
is quite different from the CI from the actual distribution of $M$:

```{r}
quantile(M, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

## Bootstrap
Bootstrap: resample $X$ with replacement to approximate the distribution of $M$:

```{r}
B <- 10^4
M_star <- replicate(B, {
  X_star <- sample(X, N, replace = TRUE)
  median(X_star)
})
```

The bootstrap CI is much closer to the true one:

```{r}
quantile(M_star, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

## Bootstrap
\Large
For more, including bias corrections for bootstrap CIs, see Efron & Tibshirani, _An Introduction to the Bootstrap_.


*In cross validation, we can bootstrap many times instead of dividing the data into equal folds.*


## The caret package {#caret}
\Large
Every ML package in R has its own syntax. __caret__ gives one consistent interface to 237 methods^[https://topepo.github.io/caret/available-models.html].
\vskip .2in

__caret__ does not install the underlying packages; the manual lists what each method needs.

## The caret `train` function 
\Large
__caret__ can also run cross validation for us. We use the 2 or 7 example again:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(dslabs)
data("mnist_27")
```

## The caret `train` function 
\Large
`train` fits different algorithms with the same syntax:

```{r}
library(caret)
train_glm <- train(y ~ ., method = "glm", 
                   data = mnist_27$train)
train_knn <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn",
                   data = mnist_27$train)
```

## The caret `train` function 
\Large
Prediction code is also the same for every method (`predict.train`):
```{r}
y_hat_glm <- predict(train_glm, 
                     mnist_27$test, type = "raw")
y_hat_knn <- predict(train_knn, 
                     mnist_27$test, type = "raw")
```

## The caret `train` function 
\Large
So comparing algorithms is quick:
```{r}
confusionMatrix(y_hat_glm, 
      mnist_27$test$y)$overall[["Accuracy"]]
confusionMatrix(y_hat_knn,
      mnist_27$test$y)$overall[["Accuracy"]]
```

## Cross validation {#caret-cv}
\Large
For algorithms with tuning parameters, `train` automatically cross validates over a few default values. To see which parameters are tuned:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
getModelInfo("knn")
```

## Cross validation {#caret-cv}
\Large
or the quicker:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
modelLookup("knn")
```

Run with defaults:
```{r}
train_knn <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn", 
                   data = mnist_27$train)
```

## Cross validation 
Plot the CV results; `highlight = TRUE` marks the best:

```{r caret-highlight, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
ggplot(train_knn, highlight = TRUE)
```

## Cross validation 
\Large
Defaults: 25 bootstrap samples, and for kNN only $k=5,7,9$.

Change the candidates with `tuneGrid`: a data frame whose column names match `modelLookup`.

## Cross validation 
\Large
Try 32 values of $k$ from 9 to 71: `data.frame(k = seq(9, 71, 2))`.

That is $32 \times 25 = 800$ kNN fits.

## Cross validation 
\Large
Cross validation is random, so set the seed for reproducibility:

```{r eval=F}
set.seed(2008)
train_knn <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn", 
      data = mnist_27$train,
      tuneGrid = data.frame(k = seq(9, 71, 2)))
ggplot(train_knn, highlight = TRUE)
```

## Cross validation 
```{r train-knn-plot1, echo=F, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="90%",fig.align="center"}
set.seed(2008)
train_knn <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn", 
                   data = mnist_27$train,
                   tuneGrid = data.frame(k = seq(9, 71, 2)))
ggplot(train_knn, highlight = TRUE)
```


## Cross validation 
\Large
The best parameter:

```{r}
train_knn$bestTune
```

## Cross validation 
\Large
and the best model:

```{r}
train_knn$finalModel
```

## Cross validation 
\Large
`predict` uses the best model. Test-set accuracy (the test set was not used in cross validation):
```{r}
confusionMatrix(predict(train_knn, 
                        mnist_27$test, type = "raw"),
                mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```

## Cross validation 
\Large
`trainControl` changes the CV method; 10-fold is faster than 25 bootstraps:
```{r cv-10-fold-accuracy-estimate, eval=F, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
control <- trainControl(method = "cv", 
               number = 10, p = .9)
train_knn_cv <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn", 
              data = mnist_27$train,
              tuneGrid = data.frame(k = seq(9, 71, 2)),
              trControl = control)
ggplot(train_knn_cv, highlight = TRUE)
```

## Cross validation 
```{r cv-10-fold-accuracy-estimate1, echo=F, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="90%",fig.align="center"}
control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, p = .9)
train_knn_cv <- train(y ~ ., method = "knn", 
                   data = mnist_27$train,
                   tuneGrid = data.frame(k = seq(9, 71, 2)),
                   trControl = control)
ggplot(train_knn_cv, highlight = TRUE)
```

## Cross validation 
\Large
Accuracy with standard deviation bars from the CV samples:

```{r accuracy-with-sd-bars, eval=F, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="70%",fig.align="center"}
train_knn$results %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = k, y = Accuracy)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = k, 
                    ymin = Accuracy - AccuracySD, 
                    ymax = Accuracy + AccuracySD))
```


## Cross validation 
```{r accuracy-with-sd-bars1, echo=F, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 6, out.width="90%",fig.align="center"}
train_knn$results %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = k, y = Accuracy)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = k, 
                    ymin = Accuracy - AccuracySD, 
                    ymax = Accuracy + AccuracySD))
```

## Example: fitting with loess

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%",fig.align="center"}
plot_cond_prob <- function(p_hat=NULL){
  tmp <- mnist_27$true_p
  if(!is.null(p_hat)){
    tmp <- mutate(tmp, p=p_hat)
  }
  tmp %>% ggplot(aes(x_1, x_2, z=p, fill=p)) +
  geom_raster(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=c("#F8766D","white","#00BFC4")) +
  stat_contour(breaks=c(0.5),color="black")
}
```

The best kNN model approximates the true conditional probability:
```{r mnist27-optimal-knn-fit, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
plot_cond_prob(predict(train_knn, mnist_27$true_p, type = "prob")[,2])
```

## Example: fitting with loess
\Large
But the boundary is wiggly: kNN, like a bin smoother, uses no kernel. Loess is smoother; in __caret__ it is the `gamLoess` method^[https://topepo.github.io/caret/available-models.html], which needs the __gam__ package:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("gam")
```

## Example: fitting with loess
It has two tuning parameters:

```{r}
modelLookup("gamLoess")
```

We tune `span` and fix `degree = 1` (the grid still needs both columns):

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(span = seq(0.15, 0.65, len = 10)
                    , degree = 1)
```

## Example: fitting with loess
\Large
Using the default CV settings:
```{r loess-accuracy, eval=F, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
train_loess <- train(y ~ ., method = "gamLoess", 
                   tuneGrid=grid,
                   data = mnist_27$train)
ggplot(train_loess, highlight = TRUE)
```


## Example: fitting with loess
```{r loess-accuracy1, echo=F, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
train_loess <- train(y ~ ., method = "gamLoess", 
                   tuneGrid=grid,
                   data = mnist_27$train)
ggplot(train_loess, highlight = TRUE)
```

## Example: fitting with loess
\Large
Accuracy is similar to kNN:
```{r}
confusionMatrix(data = predict(
      train_loess, mnist_27$test), 
      reference = mnist_27$test$y)$overall["Accuracy"]
```

## Example: fitting with loess
but the estimate is smoother:

```{r gam-smooth, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%",fig.align="center"}
p1 <- plot_cond_prob() + ggtitle("True conditional probability")

p2 <- plot_cond_prob(predict(train_loess, mnist_27$true_p, type = "prob")[,2]) + 
  ggtitle("GAM Loess estimate")

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p2, p1, nrow=1)
```


## Application: developing a TB biomarker
\Large
Back to the TB NanoString data: 179 people (active TB vs. latent infection), 107 genes.

* $p$ (107 genes) is close to $N$ (179 people): easy to overfit
* Goal: a classifier that works on **new** patients
* Cross-validation is how we choose and honestly evaluate it

\normalsize
```{r tb-load}
tb <- readRDS("TBnanostring.rds")
tb$TB_Status <- factor(tb$TB_Status, levels = c("LTBI", "TB"))
```

## kNN on all 107 genes, tuned by CV
\small
```{r tb-knn, fig.show='hide'}
set.seed(1)
idx <- createDataPartition(tb$TB_Status, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
tb_train <- tb[idx, ]; tb_test <- tb[-idx, ]
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)
fit_knn <- train(TB_Status ~ ., data = tb_train, method = "knn",
                 preProcess = c("center", "scale"), metric = "ROC",
                 tuneGrid = data.frame(k = seq(3, 75, 6)), trControl = ctrl)
fit_knn$bestTune
```

## kNN on all 107 genes, tuned by CV
```{r tb-knn-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="55%", fig.width=6, fig.height=3.8, fig.align='center'}
plot(fit_knn)
```

\Large
Cross-validated AUC for each $k$; `train` picks the best and refits on all the training data.

## Checking on the test set
\normalsize
```{r tb-knn-test}
p_knn <- predict(fit_knn, tb_test, type = "prob")[, "TB"]
pROC::auc(pROC::roc(tb_test$TB_Status, p_knn, levels = c("LTBI", "TB"),
                    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
confusionMatrix(predict(fit_knn, tb_test), tb_test$TB_Status,
                positive = "TB")$byClass[c("Sensitivity", "Specificity")]
```

\Large
The CV estimate (`r round(max(fit_knn$results$ROC), 2)`) and the test AUC are close: CV gave a fair estimate without touching the test set.

## A common pitfall: selecting genes before CV
\Large
A tempting shortcut:

1. Use **all** samples to find the 10 genes that best separate TB from LTBI
2. Then cross-validate a classifier built on those 10 genes

The CV error is now **optimistic**: the test folds already helped choose the genes. This **selection bias** has inflated many published biomarkers (Ambroise & McLachlan, *PNAS*, 2002).

## Demonstrating selection bias
Shuffle the labels so **no** gene is truly related to TB status, then compare selecting genes outside vs. inside the CV loop:
\scriptsize
```{r tb-selbias}
X <- scale(as.matrix(tb[, -1]))
score_cv <- function(X, y, inside, ntop = 10) {
  pick <- function(Xs, ys) {                 # top genes by t-statistic
    t <- apply(Xs, 2, function(g) t.test(g[ys == "TB"], g[ys == "LTBI"])$statistic)
    top <- order(abs(t), decreasing = TRUE)[1:ntop]
    list(top = top, sign = sign(t[top])) }
  folds <- createFolds(y, k = 5); p <- numeric(length(y))
  if (!inside) sel <- pick(X, y)             # WRONG: uses all samples
  for (f in folds) {
    if (inside) sel <- pick(X[-f, ], y[-f])  # RIGHT: training folds only
    p[f] <- X[f, sel$top, drop = FALSE] %*% sel$sign }
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(y, p, levels = c("LTBI", "TB"),
                                 direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))) }
set.seed(1)
res <- replicate(20, { y_shuffled <- sample(tb$TB_Status)
  c(outside = score_cv(X, y_shuffled, FALSE), inside = score_cv(X, y_shuffled, TRUE)) })
round(rowMeans(res), 2)
```

## Demonstrating selection bias
\Large
With labels that carry **no** information:

* Genes selected **outside** CV: AUC $\approx$ `r round(rowMeans(res)["outside"], 2)`, a "biomarker" out of pure noise
* Genes selected **inside** CV: AUC $\approx$ `r round(rowMeans(res)["inside"], 2)`, correctly a coin flip
* With the real labels (inside CV): AUC $\approx$ `r round(score_cv(X, tb$TB_Status, TRUE), 2)`

## Biomarker development: lessons
\Large
* Every data-driven step (gene selection, scaling, tuning) goes **inside** the CV loop (caret: `preProcess`, `sbf`, `rfe`)
* Keep a test set untouched until the model is **locked**
* Then validate in an **independent cohort** (different site, time, or population)
* Small studies give noisy estimates: report confidence intervals

## Summary
\large
* Training error is optimistic; we need an honest estimate of test error
* Small $k$ in kNN over-trains; large $k$ over-smooths
* K-fold CV and the bootstrap estimate test error from the training data
* Tune parameters by CV; keep the test set for the final check
* caret's `train` handles resampling and tuning for hundreds of models
* Biomarkers: put gene selection inside CV, lock the model, then validate in an independent cohort
